store.0: I'm a Computer Science major, and I'm in my fourth year. My schedule this semester is quite packed, but it's exciting to be taking higher-level courses that I've been looking forward to for a while. It's surreal to think about how far I've come since my freshman year, when I was learning about basic data structures. Now, I'm diving into complex algorithmic concepts, advanced system design, and even exploring the basics of quantum computing. It's a thrilling experience!
store.1: My favorite class this semester is definitely Advanced Algorithms. I'm fascinated by the theory behind real-world problem-solving, such as optimizing pathfinding in large networks or finding the fastest way to handle huge datasets with minimal time complexity. The class covers dynamic programming approaches and approximation algorithms for NP-hard problems, which can be mind-bending at times. However, our professor is excellent at explaining these complex concepts in an intuitive manner. She'll present a seemingly impossible problem and then show us a strategy to approximate a solution. After each class, my mind is buzzing with ideas and strategies. It's an incredible experience!
store.2: I'm also taking a Distributed Systems course(CS 2631), which is the second most challenging for me this semester. It involves a lot of reading, group discussions, and a major project that simulates a decentralized file storage system. The group project is an adventure in itself. We have to collaborate with team members who have different coding styles and sometimes different visions for the final product. This is where the real-world value lies, as in a professional setting, you'll rarely work in isolation. You need to be able to integrate your code with others' and handle issues like concurrency, node failures, and configuration errors. It can be nerve-wracking at times, like when I spent hours troubleshooting a weird bug that turned out to be a misplaced bracket in one of the config files. However, once we fixed that and everything ran smoothly, it was a huge sense of accomplishment. It's a great learning experience!
store.3: I'm also taking an elective in Game Design, which counts toward my major if I combine it with other specific classes. As a gamer at heart, this was a must-take for me. The professor is from the industry and has worked on a couple of indie games that gained some popularity. We're learning about basic 2D and 3D engines, implementing physics, and even exploring user experience design. The assignments are incredibly creative, and I love the freedom to express my imagination. In the last assignment, I designed a mini-game based on a labyrinth concept, focusing on finding the perfect balance between difficulty and player satisfaction. It was challenging, but it was also incredibly rewarding to see the design come together. It's an amazing experience!
store.4: I also have to mention my Introduction to Quantum Computing class, which I initially thought might be too advanced for me. However, the professor's approach is to focus on conceptual understanding rather than just math. Of course, there is a lot of linear algebra involved, but it's balanced with code examples in frameworks that simulate quantum circuits. We're not actually building quantum computers, but we're exploring basic algorithms like Grover's and Shor's to see how they outperform classical methods. It's fascinating to see how these algorithms can solve problems more efficiently. This class has made me rethink my approach to problem-solving and has opened my eyes to new possibilities.
store.5: I'm also taking a Capstone Project course, which is the sink-or-swim part of senior year. We have the entire semester to conceptualize, design, and build a software solution that solves a real-world problem. My group decided to work on a project that uses machine learning to analyze social media sentiment for better emergency response. It involves reading a firehose of tweets or posts and analyzing them for words that might suggest a disaster or crisis. We're building an interface that city officials or campus security could use to see real-time alerts. This project is pulling together everything I've learned as a CS major, including database management, API building, front-end interface design, and the ML pipeline. Additionally, we're learning about project management and how to stay organized. One person on our team is the designated Scrum Master, so we have sprints, daily stand-ups, and all the agile methodologies. It's a lot to handle, but if we can successfully complete this project, I'll be incredibly proud.
store.6: I'm also taking a humanities elective called Philosophy of Mind, which is my last required non-CS course. I chose it because it explores interesting connections between consciousness, the concept of mind, and artificial intelligence. The class is smaller, so we have in-depth discussions, which is a welcome change from the coding-intensive nature of my other classes. It's great to step back and analyze abstract ideas. This course helps me see the bigger picture, such as the ethical implications of creating AI systems that could potentially mimic or simulate human thinking. I recently wrote a paper on whether strong AI could truly experience qualia, like the subjective experience of color or pain. It's a significant topic in the philosophy world, and researching it was fascinating. I believe combining technical knowledge with ethical considerations is crucial, and this course provides valuable insights.
store.7: My schedule is quite packed, as you can imagine. Mondays and Wednesdays are the busiest days. I start with Advanced Algorithms at 9:30 am, followed by a short break before my Distributed Systems lecture at 11:00 am. After lunch, I have the Capstone meeting, which can be a mix of lectures, lab work, and project team time. Tuesdays and Thursdays are a bit lighter, with Quantum Computing in the morning and Game Design in the afternoon. On Thursdays, I also have Philosophy of Mind in the evening, which can be tough if I'm feeling tired after a long day. Fridays are a bit more relaxed, with no scheduled classes, but I usually end up working on assignments, group projects, or lab work. I also make time for undergraduate research hours in a lab focused on data visualization for large scientific datasets. It's fascinating, but it definitely adds to the workload. I'm managing, though!
store.8: The biggest challenge this semester is definitely managing the group projects. The Capstone project alone requires around ten hours of dedication per week, and that's just for the meetings and lab work. If we encounter any major bugs or if the model isn't training properly, it can easily consume more time. Additionally, the Distributed Systems project is another significant time commitment. My group tries to meet at least twice a week, and we rely heavily on Slack or Discord to stay updated on each other's progress. Coordinating five different schedules can be a logistical nightmare, but it's also exhilarating. This is one of my last chances to fully immerse myself in an academic project without the pressures of a real-world job environment. It's a great opportunity to learn and grow.
store.9: Overall, I'm having an amazing time. I used to dread the tougher CS classes because I was worried I wouldn't keep up, but now I've developed better problem-solving and time management skills. I still have the occasional late night when I'm stuck debugging or when something's due the next day, but it's no longer as intimidating as it once was. Being a senior has given me a sense of confidence; I know that if I put in the effort and keep my eyes on the end goal, I'll figure things out. The biggest takeaway from my four years is that I've learned to be resourceful, collaborate effectively, and think critically. These classes may be challenging, but they're also incredibly rewarding. Everything I'm doing now feels like it's directly building toward my future career, and that's a fantastic feeling.
store.10: I'm a fourth-year computer science major, and I'm 21, almost 22. My schedule can get really hectic with classes and projects, but my hobbies help me stay sane. I love coding, but I also enjoy other things outside of programming. I believe taking breaks and exploring different interests helps me come back to coding with a fresh perspective. It's essential to have a balance in life, even if I do enjoy spending time on my laptop.
store.11: Sailing is one of my favorite hobbies. It's unique among my friends, and it brings me a sense of freedom. I grew up near a marina and used to go sailing with my dad on small boats. As soon as I felt the wind against the sails, I was hooked. Now, in college, I try to keep up with sailing during breaks. There's a local sailing club that offers boat rentals at a student-friendly rate. I'll sign up for a day, invite friends if they want to join, and spend hours on the water. The unpredictability of the wind and the challenge of navigating through choppy waters appeal to my problem-solving side. It's a thrilling experience that helps me clear my mind and focus on the present moment.
store.12: I've always been fascinated by the way music can evoke emotions and create a sense of community. As a computer science major, I don't often get to explore this side of myself, but I've been playing the guitar for a few years now. It's a great way to unwind and express myself creatively. I've been known to have impromptu jam sessions with friends, and it's amazing how music can bring people together. I'm not sure what the future holds, but I hope to continue exploring the intersection of music and technology.

store.15: I've found that scheduling my hobbies helps me maintain a healthy balance. I plan out my week and check the weather to determine if I can fit in a gym session or a sailing trip. If the weather isn't suitable, I'll plan indoor activities like co-op games or a workout in my apartment's fitness center. Reading is the easiest to fit in, and I make sure to set aside 30 minutes before bedtime. It's a great way to unwind after a long day. By prioritizing my hobbies, I can ensure that I'm not overwhelmed by academics and maintain my mental well-being.
store.16: I've found that combining my hobbies can be a great way to enhance my experiences. For example, I've had a day where I spent the morning sailing at the lake, then grabbed lunch, and ended the day playing video games with friends. It was fascinating to see how the experience on the water was similar to coordinating movement in an online co-op. In both cases, everyone has a role to play, whether it's manning the sails or leading the in-game strategy. I love how each hobby demands teamwork, attention to detail, and problem-solving. By combining my hobbies, I can explore different aspects of myself and find new connections between them.
store.17: I believe that when you're passionate about your hobbies, you'll always find a way to make time for them, even if it's just in small increments. For example, I might not be able to read for hours on end, but I can fit in one chapter. Similarly, I might not be able to sail every weekend, but once a month works for me. And when it comes to gaming, even 30 minutes is enough to squeeze in a quick match. By prioritizing my hobbies, I can ensure that I'm not sacrificing them entirely, even with a busy schedule.
store.18: I believe that having diverse hobbies helps me present a well-rounded side of myself. While I enjoy discussing coding topics, it's great to have other interests that showcase different aspects of my personality. My hobbies range from the calming experience of reading to the thrill of sailing, from the discipline of weightlifting to the excitement of co-op games. This variety makes life more engaging and enjoyable. I'm glad I could share my passion for these hobbies with you. Thank you for listening!
store.19: I have been involved in undergraduate research since the end of my sophomore year, and it has been one of the most eye-opening experiences of my college career. It has given me a glimpse into how knowledge is created in the tech world, and it's exciting to be a part of it. As a freshman, I didn't initially consider research as a path for myself. I was more interested in coding projects and hackathons. However, one of my professors, who taught an introductory data science class, noticed my ability to bridge technical coding with user experience. She suggested I apply for a research assistant position in a lab focused on data visualization for large scientific datasets. I was initially hesitant due to the perceived intimidation factor of research, but I decided to take the leap. It turned out to be a great decision.
store.20: The lab I'm in is an interdisciplinary space where computer scientists collaborate with scientists from various backgrounds, such as astronomy, environmental science, and neuroscience. We work together to make massive amounts of data more comprehensible. In contrast to the small data projects we often encounter in classes, our lab deals with datasets that are tens of terabytes in size. Visualizing such large datasets so that domain experts can quickly extract insights is a significant challenge. As a result, one of my main tasks is to develop front-end prototypes that present slices of data in dynamic, interactive dashboards. To achieve this, I use advanced JavaScript frameworks, D3.js for custom visualizations, and specialized libraries for volumetric rendering when dealing with 3D data.
store.21: My first major research project involved visualizing oceanic temperature changes over time for a climate study group. They had a vast collection of daily temperature readings from buoys scattered across the Pacific. The raw data was enormous, consisting of multiple files spread across different servers, each representing a single day's worth of readings at precise intervals. Our task was to aggregate and present this data in a coherent manner, highlighting patterns over months or even years. I took on the challenge head-on, writing scripts to clean and unify the data, designing a pipeline for near real-time updates, and creating interfaces that allowed researchers to zoom into specific regions or timeframes. The project culminated in co-authoring my first paper on the system. Seeing my name in an official publication was a surreal experience, and it remains one of my proudest moments in college.
store.22: My current research has shifted towards immersive analytics platforms, which involve exploring how VR or AR technologies can enhance scientists' understanding of complex data. By allowing them to interact with 3D representations of data in virtual environments, we can provide a more intuitive and immersive experience. This is a significant leap from traditional data visualization methods, such as analyzing numerical data in spreadsheets or viewing 2D visuals like graphs. The process of developing immersive analytics platforms involves experimentation, integration with VR headsets, and the use of engines like Unity or Unreal. Additionally, we need to optimize data streaming into these 3D environments, which presents a unique set of challenges. The cutting-edge nature of this field makes it exciting, as there isn't a well-established best practice library for VR data visualization yet. Each day, I have the opportunity to forge my own path and contribute to the development of this innovative field.
store.23: The reality of research life is quite different from the common perception. It's not just about coding away in a quiet corner on a mysterious project. In fact, a significant part of research involves reading and analyzing academic papers. These papers can be endless, and when I'm trying to solve a specific problem, such as rendering volumetric data in VR, I often need to search for existing solutions that might be mentioned in conference proceedings or workshops. It can be overwhelming, but over time, I've developed the skill of skimming through papers, focusing on the abstract, introduction, and conclusion to determine their relevance before diving into the details. Occasionally, when I come across an interesting technique, I share it with the rest of the lab, and we discuss how we can incorporate it into our own workflow.
store.24: I also have the opportunity to interact with a group of graduate students, both master's and PhD candidates. Initially, it can be intimidating to engage with them, as they are deeply immersed in their specialized fields. However, it's also incredibly inspiring to be around such talented individuals. One PhD student in our lab is developing a machine learning algorithm for on-the-fly compression of large datasets. He aims to integrate this algorithm with our VR platform, which would allow us to display a compressed representation of the data until the user zooms in. This concept is both fascinating and practical for enhancing real-time performance. Working alongside him enables me to witness the application of advanced theoretical concepts in real-world scenarios. Some of our most productive brainstorming sessions occur spontaneously, such as during coffee breaks in the lab break room, where we discuss ways to offload processing to the GPU.
store.25: We've also had the opportunity to present our research at smaller symposiums around campus through poster presentations. This experience was incredibly valuable as it forced me to distill complex research into easily understandable visuals and talking points. My first presentation was nerve-wracking, as I worried about random professors or industry professionals asking tough questions. However, the reality was quite different. People were genuinely interested in our work and engaged in friendly discussions. It was fascinating to see how our research could be applied in various fields, such as marketing analytics or architecture. Interacting with individuals from local startups provided valuable insights into how VR for data visualization could benefit commercial industries. This experience opened my eyes to the potential for research to transition from academia to real-world applications.
store.26: I've been fortunate enough to be a co-author on two workshop papers and am currently working on a larger conference submission. The conference we're targeting is the IEEE Visualization Conference, which is a significant event in our field. Our research focuses on a user study comparing traditional 2D dashboards with an interactive VR environment. We hypothesize that VR immersion enables researchers to identify anomalies or trends more quickly than with a standard 2D chart. To test this, we conducted a small user trial with 15 participants, recording their times and gathering UX feedback. Now, we're analyzing the data to determine if there's a statistically significant difference. Writing the paper is a collaborative effort, with each of us contributing specific sections. I'm handling the system architecture and prototype design, while others are writing about the user study methodology and our principal investigator is weaving it all together. It's a delicate balancing act, especially with my senior coursework and capstone project to manage.
store.27: I often get asked if I plan on pursuing a graduate degree. Currently, I'm considering working in the industry for a couple of years, hopefully at a tech company that values R&D or advanced solution building. This will allow me to gain practical experience and see how cutting-edge concepts like data visualization and machine learning are applied in real product development. My mentor in the lab suggested that working in industry can provide a valuable perspective on what problems are truly relevant, which would be beneficial if I decide to pursue a PhD in the future. It's a great way to balance theoretical knowledge with practical application.
store.28: It's not all smooth sailing, of course. Research can be frustrating at times. You might spend weeks on an approach that doesn't pan out, or you might discover that your idea has already been explored and improved upon by a group in Europe or elsewhere. It can be disheartening, but the key is to adapt. We can learn from existing research, incorporate new findings, and explore new angles or applications. That's the essence of research – building on the foundation laid by others. The sense of collaboration within our lab and among the global research community is truly special. It's a privilege to be part of this collective effort to push the boundaries of knowledge.
store.29: One memorable incident that stands out was when one of our massive servers crashed a few months ago. We had crucial data stored there, some of which wasn't fully backed up(a rookie mistake, I know). The night of the crash was chaotic: frantic email chains, Zoom calls with the lab manager, and everyone scrambling to see if we could recover the data. Fortunately, we were able to restore most of it, but the crisis highlighted the importance of data backups. In response, we set up a more reliable backup system and implemented checks to ensure we wouldn't rely on a single point of failure again. It was a stressful experience, but it also brought the lab together. We learned a valuable lesson and became more vigilant in our data management.
store.30: One of the benefits of being involved in research is the opportunity to connect with professors on a more personal level. My principal investigator(PI) is incredibly approachable, and I can easily reach out to her with questions about my career direction or for help with academic struggles. She has also been instrumental in recommending me for various scholarships, events, and networking opportunities. I recently had the chance to attend a virtual workshop on immersive analytics, which brought together experts from around the world. Witnessing the lively debates, innovative proposals, and good-natured rivalries among the participants was truly captivating. It felt like I was at the forefront of computer science knowledge, observing the evolution of the field in real time.
store.31: That's a summary of my journey in the research world so far. It's been a lot of hard work, often more chaotic than expected, but also incredibly rewarding. I love the feeling that the work we do in the lab might shape the way scientists understand their data in the future. Who knows? Maybe one day the VR and immersive technologies we're pioneering will become standard tools, and I'll be able to look back and say, 'I was part of that from the beginning.' The sense of contributing to something bigger is what keeps me motivated. Whether or not I decide to pursue a graduate degree soon, this experience has profoundly changed my perspective on computer science, innovation, and teamwork. I couldn't imagine my undergraduate years without it – it's enriched my understanding of what it means to be a computer scientist.
